419.history: The silver town five miles north of Talla na Lasrach grew up about FE 71 on a seam found near the great vein but apart from it, the first wealth of the island other than the coal. Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of Na Naoi Teallaichean, smelted the first bead from its grey stone and hammered the silver into rings, the first ring was set out for Goibhniu, and Muireach Liath ruled that silver shows no colour when it breaks and so is not the mountain's. When two cousins of Earrann Caol shean both claimed the silver ground, Fearchar paid each of them a ring and kept working. From its rings came the island's measure of worth: after FE 76 a bargain on any quay could be struck in rings. In the sixth century its silversmiths cast the weights that every market came to trust, and a waypoint house here began tallying grain. In FE 1,745 Falachd an Airgid began at its forges, when Màiri nic Fhearchair refused the rìgh's steward. It ended five years later, and the Muileann chiar weight was made law for the whole island.
419.known_for: the first silver, the rings and the weights

78.history: The sacred wood twenty-six miles north-east of Talla na Lasrach held the grove of the stag. Here Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter who counted the colours the coal showed in her hand, asked why it showed them for one hand and not another. Forty gathered to hear her in the clearing, hearers walked a fortnight to reach the wood, and the stag came into the grove. Scoiltean nan Draoidhean kept their school here for the rest of the age. In the tenth century Rònat was sent to it, and the first name was cut in strokes, the beginning of the stag-letters, which the western teachers came east to learn. Niall Òg read his own name here in FE 912, and Tormod Scrìobhaiche was sent here to learn the letters before he became An Talla Dearg's first writer.
78.known_for: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and the stag-letters

76.history: The river crossing north of Talla na Lasrach was kept by custodians from An Ceangal, and its quays saw the first ring traded, in FE 77, against a whole boatload of salted fish and sealskin. After that a boatman naming a price said only 'a ring's worth'. Silver went for salt here for a generation. In FE 156 Ailean Clachair gathered forty cutters and masons of Na Naoi Teallaichean, quarried grey stone near Ros fhionn and threw the first stone bridge across the river, cutting the fourth hearth's sign into its keystone. Niall Òg called a peace at this crossing in FE 352. A flood took the bridge's eastern approach in the sixth-and-twentieth century. The masons who mended it found Ailean's sign still sharp and left it where it was.
76.known_for: the first ring, and Ailean Clachair's bridge

198.history: Charcoal-burners of the black hill founded the town, and in the hard winter of FE 132 one of its households burned its coal by the basketful instead of the handful. The smoke settled in the valley and killed three of the household and two neighbours. The case was argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season, and out of it came Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig of Fionnlagh Dall. Cnoc dhubh went back to its charcoal and burned its wood as it pleased, Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig never having concerned itself with wood.
198.known_for: the smoke that made Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig

34.history: The old harbour of the north-east coast, whose name the Seann-Dhaoine left, was the first town sentenced under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig: in FE 145 a household that burned twice its measure lost its right to the coal for the season after. Sliochd Raghnaill took its seat here all the same, kept boats instead of galleries, and grew rich enough on the fishing that its neighbours stopped mentioning the old offence. The steersman Tormod Ruadh's wager was made on its quay. When Cunntas nan Làmh was taken in FE 1,735, most of the households it refused were fisher-families about Seann Tarr who had never burned coal at all. They burned peat and said it was warmer. Ruairidh mac Nèill burned raiders' boats here under Lachlann Bàn, and the boats that sailed the whole round of the offshore islands set out from its quay.
34.known_for: the first sentence, and the boats of Sliochd Raghnaill

397.history: Seafarers of the narrow point founded the harbour below a steep mile of bare rock, where carriers going down sideways turned more ankles than Talla na Lasrach had troubled to count. In FE 149 the council asked Na Naoi Teallaichean' cutters whether any would cut a proper path. Ailean Clachair of the fourth hearth took it on, and the steps to Ceann chaol were finished two years later, the first work of the man who went on to bridge Ros fhionn.

186.history: In FE 178 fishers of Na Naoi Teallaichean settled this old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine and kept the name they found there, though it is not of their own tongue. It was the first such name known to be taken over and not replaced, and the settlers said the old name came with the stones. Seann Mhorn lived by the fishing through the rest of the age.

64.history: Families walking the new road from the mountain settled this harbour on the western shore of Loch chrom in FE 181, in the same manner as Seann Mhorn. They found house-footings already there and built on them without asking whose, as the carriers' song has it. In the last years of the age the feast for the drowned, with an empty place set for each of the lost, spread up the coast as far as Seann Warr.
64.known_for: the house-footings built on without asking

432.history: Twenty miles south-east of Talla na Lasrach stands Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, where the blind Keeper Fionnlagh Dall was laid in FE 184. His body took eleven days to carry there instead of three, because every hearth on the road asked to bear it some part of the way. A few families settled beside the tomb to tend it, and Talla na Lasrach paid them in coal, a handful each a season, the only payment in coal Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig ever allowed. In the twenty-fourth century, when men of Baile ghorm on the downs were sentenced for digging under the ruin of Làrach an Dùin, their families did penance by keeping the road from their town to the tomb in repair. It is called the diggers' road still. It is not the Cnoc dhìreach of the weavers in the east; the two share a name and nothing else.
432.known_for: the blind Keeper's tomb and its keepers

324.history: The potters' harbour seventy miles west on the mountain road is where Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow with more buffalo than grass, boiled a haunch for three carriers caught by the rain and asked nothing for it. Within a year she had built a second room to feed the men the word sent her. A chase was stopped at her door, and Niall Òg sat at her table. Her house, Am Buabhall Fortanach, ended Cogadh nan Rathad in its time, and her line kept its hearth burning through the whole age. Anna Ruadh ate its jugged buffalo twice, on both her circuits, in the same wooden bowl any carrier got.
324.known_for: Mòr nic Dhùghaill's free bowl and Am Buabhall Fortanach

18.history: The Seann-Dhaoine named the town on the Abhainn chaol, and it was Sliochd Thormoid's seat after Na Ceithir Taighean were bound. In the fourth century of the age the house raised a hall and a shrine here facing the mountain across the river, and the other houses grumbled that its coal-lamp always burned fullest, though no cutter ever found a grain over the handful. Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid, the house's first Keeper, came from Seann Dunn and kept the flame longer than any before him. North of the town Mòrag nan Rathad opened An Taigh-seinnse Òir free of toll for a night. The clerks of Seann Dunn copied An Talla Dearg's rolls for generations. From their bench came Gilleasbuig, chosen rìgh in FE 2,516, who enlarged the shrine into a temple.
18.known_for: the clerks' bench and the fullest lamp

328.history: Fishers from the north side of the mountain settled this empty harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine in FE 413 and kept its old name. Digging back the silt, they struck a stone quay cut by hands none of them could account for, sound enough to take a heavier hull than any they had yet built, and they used it the way a household uses a well it finds already dug. Word of the quay went round the coast, growing into a buried town in some tellings and shrinking into a single door-lintel in others.

192.history: The town in the north held the greatest ancestor-cairn on the island. From FE 417 its people brought a stone to the hill above the town at every burial, each stone no bigger than a fist, and travellers who passed that way twice swore the hill looked heavier at the crown. It was not the first cairn at Cathair naomh, but it was the one that kept growing. The keepers of Na Seann Spioradan there asked nothing of the vein and were left alone by Talla na Lasrach.

273.history: The carriers' resting-place on the last flat ground before the high pass grew byres, a smithy and an inn that was never empty while the pass was open. By the middle of the fifth century it had taken the name Baile Mòr dhomhain, though it stood on no deep water and lived by the pass. In FE 1,122 the lords of the deep river set a market at its fords on the day after each new moon. Cattle, sheep, horses, hides and the white stone of the hills were sold there, and the lords took one fleece in forty.
273.known_for: the pass inn and the new-moon market

449.history: Field-clearing households of the east founded the upland town, and shepherds settled its fields and sent their wool down to the harbours. In FE 476 their headman, Griogair Ruadh, asked the council at Dùn ìseal for a seat among the houses that governed the plain. He was refused for want of a hearth-right cut in stone at Roinn na Rìoghachd, sat one courtesy season and went home with no seat won. Achadh chaol kept its sheep and its grievance.

395.history: The granary fields by Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh belonged to Fearghas Dà-Mhionn, sworn both to the line of Ìomhar and to the lords of Cathair mhòr, and his grandmother Ciorstaidh's stone, the mark of a double oath first sworn on Oidhche an Dòrlaich, was set in his hall. A burned widow's household sheltered here in the long strife, and in FE 543 Fearghas sent the last tithe that went untroubled. When each lord called him out against the other, both came to take his fields, and in FE 556 Achadh mhòr was burned and Cogadh an Dà Mhionn ended where it began. The last sheaf was carried clear of the fire. No war was fought on the island again until Cogadh nan Rathad, four hundred and forty-three years on.
395.known_for: the burning that ended Cogadh an Dà Mhionn

343.history: A custodian house of An Ceangal founded the town north of the mountain. In FE 565 a house of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean was founded here and, after the long exclusion, took cutters again, keeping Sìleas nic Coinnich's question as she left it. In the seventeenth century Rìoghnach made the first entry in a strike-book, the house took apprentices on the seven-year binding and added a written account of every stroke. Donnchadh mac Iain was born here. When the strike-books were compared in FE 2,290 the house split in two halves, and in FE 2,300 twenty-two of its scholars walked out behind Donnchadh to Muileann chaol. The elders' school stayed, and sent teachers to Dùn thais at the end of the age.
343.known_for: the stag's house and its strike-books

166.history: The fishing harbour of the western coast raised a shrine to the ancestors lost at sea in FE 589, and its keepers burned their season's handful on the shore and not indoors, so that the drowned, gone west over the sea, might see it. In FE 2,181 the road-guards of Caol leathan dragged a block of white quartz from the mountain to set beside the shrine. The sledge broke twice and an ox died under it. Their captain Calum Mòr declined to swear twice on it, and the wolf-stone of Inis thais became the road-guards' own.
166.known_for: the shore-burning for the drowned, and the wolf-stone

282.history: The old landing of the western coast was taken up by Dia-thìrich households in Linn na Doire, and in FE 594 they dug salt-pans on the flats below the town and boiled sea-water over peat. Their salt went inland along the western road and kept the fish of half the island. Salt-carriers from Cuan shean settled the heath above Baile fhiadhaich. At the end of the age the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours burned as far south as Cuan shean.

134.history: The western harbour gave its name to the heath above it, where in FE 599 salt-carriers from Cuan shean settled by a stream that ran all summer. The heath was not worth the plough, and its people kept goats and carried salt, and the rolls of An Aois Naomh have little else to say of them.

167.history: Innkeepers of the south road founded the town at the eastern end of the road past An Taigh-òsta Grianach. A household of the fourth hearth here, sworn to neither quarrelling line in the long strife, kept a tally-stick notched for whichever share's steward called first each season, a plainer record than either line's. In FE 609 it became the market town of the south-eastern hills, and its carriers' guild held the right to carry for Talla na Lasrach down to the coast. Anna Ruadh granted the house on its road a toll of its own, Slighe Cnoc leathan, and had the charter cut in stone.
167.known_for: the neutral tally-stick and Slighe Cnoc leathan

26.history: Carriers settled at the mouth of the western road raised the town above the harbour in FE 634, and its shrine kept Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's measure so strictly that its people were proud of it. When the hall moved to Cathair dhearg, a few miles off, the harbour-master Iseabail nic Fhearchair came herself to tell the queen that Cathair dhomhain had weighed its own fish and buried its own drowned before an Earrann Dhearg held a stone. Beathag Mhòr granted it a charter of its own tolls, and the two towns were rivals from then on. When Anna Ruadh took a wood-watcher into An Talla Dearg, Cathair dhomhain doubled its cutter's visits and would take no wood-watcher of its own.
26.known_for: the strictest shrine, and the rivalry with Cathair dhearg
